title: Planning and Recording Investigations
seo_title: Grade 7 Science: Planning and Recording Investigations Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: Learners plan investigations by identifying and controlling variables, choose suitable equipment and units, record data accurately in tables and graphs, calculate means, and evaluate results and conclusions. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 7, Quarter 1: Science of Materials)
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 1: Science of Materials): variables, fair tests, measuring and recording data, means, graphs and evaluating conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Change one variable, measure one variable, control the rest.
key_sub: Repeat trials and find the mean.
body_html:
How to think about it

An investigation begins with a testable question and a hypothesis. The independent variable is the one you change; the dependent variable is the one you measure; controlled variables are kept the same so the test is fair.

Record data in a table with units, repeat trials and calculate the mean, and plot a graph to see the pattern. Evaluate the results: are there outliers, errors or limits? Draw a conclusion that is supported by the data.

Example

Trials: 12 s, 14 s, 13 s. Mean?

Add and divide

Answer: 13 s

Example

Testing how salt amount affects boiling point. Independent variable?

What you change

Answer: the amount of salt

Common mistakes

  • Changing more than one variable at a time.
  • Leaving units out of a table.
  • Claiming more than the data show.

items.q: A class investigates how the amount of light affects the growth of wheat seedlings. Which is the independent variable (the one you change)?
c: the same soil and the same amount of water
items.e: Change: the amount of light. Measure: the height of the seedlings. Keep the same: the same soil and the same amount of water.

items.q: A class investigates how the amount of salt in water affects how fast bean seeds sprout. Which is the dependent variable (the one you measure)?
c: the same kind of seed and the same temperature
how many days the seeds take to sprout
items.e: Change: the amount of salt. Measure: how many days the seeds take to sprout. Keep the same: the same kind of seed and the same temperature.

items.q: What does 'precise' mean for a set of measurements?
c: the results are close to each other
the results are close to the true value
items.e: Precise results have little spread.

items.q: A student measured the distance a paper plane flew four times: 4 m, 2.7 m, 2.4 m, 2.6 m. Ignoring the anomalous result, what is the mean?
items.e: The anomaly is 4 m. Mean of the other three: 7.7 ÷ 3 = 2.6 m.

items.q: How long is the pencil?

items.q: What does 'accurate' mean for a measurement?
items.e: Accuracy is about closeness to the true value.

items.q: What is a valid investigation?
c: one that tests what it is meant to test, with other variables controlled
one that gives the expected result
items.e: Valid means it answers the question fairly.

items.q: A class measured the stretch for a mass hung on a spring from 100 to 500 g. Why is it risky to predict the result for 10,000 g?

items.e: Extrapolating far beyond the data is unreliable; for example, a spring can overstretch.

items.q: A group repeated a test of the volume of gas made in 1 minute four times: 30 mL, 27 mL, 33 mL, 30 mL. What is the range of the results?
items.e: Range = largest − smallest = 33 − 27 = 6 mL.

items.q: What is a random error?
c: an error that is the same every time
an unpredictable error that makes repeated readings vary
items.e: Repeating and averaging reduces random error.

items.q: What does 'reproducible' mean?
c: other scientists get the same results when they repeat the method
items.e: Clear methods make results reproducible.

items.q: A group repeated a test of the time for a cart to roll down a ramp four times: 3.2 s, 3.5 s, 3.8 s, 3.5 s. How should the mean be reported with its uncertainty (half the range)?
items.e: Mean 3.5; half the range is 0.6 ÷ 2 = 0.3.

items.q: A survey asks only learners at one surf club about their favorite sport. Which change would best improve the investigation?
c: Repeat the test and compare means.
Survey a random sample from many schools.
Use the same beaker and volume of water.
Give every pot the same amount of water.
items.e: The sample is not representative of all learners.

items.q: A student measures the temperature of water by reading the thermometer from above at an angle. Which change would best improve the investigation?
c: Read the scale at eye level.
Use the same beaker and volume of water.
Repeat the trial to see if the result happens again.
items.e: Parallax error can make every reading wrong.

items.q: Which source is most reliable for a science report?
items.e: Peer review means other experts checked it.

Why do scientists report uncertainty, such as 4.2 ± 0.1 s?
c: to show how much the results could vary

items.q: Why should graphs have the independent variable on the x-axis?
c: it is the convention, so the graph shows how the dependent variable changes with it
items.e: The dependent variable goes on the y-axis.

items.q: A group repeated a test of the temperature rise of 100 mL of water heated for 1 minute four times: 16.5 °C, 16.5 °C, 18.0 °C, 15.0 °C. What is the range of the results?
items.e: Range = largest − smallest = 18.0 − 15.0 = 3.0 °C.

items.q: What is bias in a study?
c: a random error that cancels out
something that unfairly pushes results one way
items.e: Who pays for a study can cause bias.

items.q: A website says ice-cream sales and shark sightings both rise in summer, so ice-cream attracts sharks. What is the main problem with this claim?
c: The claim is wrong because the scientists were young.
Both are caused by hot weather; a correlation does not show cause.
Nothing is wrong; one result is enough.
The claim is proven because it was published online.
items.e: Good evidence needs a fair test, a large sample, a control and no bias.

items.q: Christian uses a data logger instead of a stopwatch. How does this improve his investigation?
c: It removes the need for a hypothesis.
It reduces human reaction-time error and records more readings.
items.e: Better equipment improves accuracy.

items.q: What is the independent variable?
c: the variables you keep the same
the variable you change on purpose
items.e: It goes on the x-axis.

items.q: Angelo repeats his test five times and gets almost the same answer each time. What does this show?
items.e: Repeatable results may still have a systematic error.

items.q: Lance's results: one trial is much higher than the rest. What should he do first?
c: check for a mistake and repeat that trial
items.e: Anomalies should be checked.

items.q: An advert says a cream 'removes wrinkles in 7 days', based on a study paid for by the cream company. What is the main problem with this claim?
c: The claim is wrong because the scientists were young.
The study may be biased, so it should be checked by independent scientists.
The claim is proven because it was published online.
The claim must be true because many people believe it.
items.e: Good evidence needs a fair test, a large sample, a control and no bias.

items.q: Lance's experiment gives results that agree closely, but his ruler was missing the first 1 cm. What kind of error is this?
items.e: Every reading is shifted by the same amount.

items.q: What is a correlation?
c: a relationship where two variables change together
proof that one variable causes another
items.e: Correlation does not always mean cause.

items.q: A sports shoe company says its shoe makes you run 20% faster, tested on its own sponsored athletes. What is the main problem with this claim?
c: The claim must be true because many people believe it.
The test is not fair or independent; the athletes may already be fast.
The claim is proven because it was published online.
The claim is wrong because the scientists were young.
items.e: Good evidence needs a fair test, a large sample, a control and no bias.

items.q: Why is a blind trial used to test a new medicine?
c: so people's expectations do not affect the results
items.e: Some people get a placebo without knowing.

items.q: A student says a new fertilizer works because her one tomato plant grew tall. What is the main problem with this claim?
c: There was no control plant without fertilizer and only one plant.
Nothing is wrong; one result is enough.
The claim must be true because many people believe it.
The claim is wrong because the scientists were young.
items.e: Good evidence needs a fair test, a large sample, a control and no bias.

items.q: Diane's hypothesis was not supported by her data. What should she do?
c: report the result honestly and suggest why
items.e: Unsupported hypotheses still teach us something.

items.q: What is a limitation of a ball-and-stick model of a molecule?
c: Real atoms are not solid balls and bonds are not sticks.
items.e: Models simplify reality.

items.q: A friend says rain always comes after his footy team wins, because it happened twice. What is the main problem with this claim?
c: The claim must be true because many people believe it.
Nothing is wrong; one result is enough.
Two events are not enough data, and there is no reason one causes the other.
The claim is wrong because the scientists were young.
items.e: Good evidence needs a fair test, a large sample, a control and no bias.
